I have been farming these 8 mu since I was a little girl helping my parents, and after forty years I know every inch of this soil. With my husband and eldest son working off-farm in the county town, I am the one who tends the fields day-to-day, though they come back to help during the busy planting and harvest peaks. I keep 5 mu in the wheat-maize rotation because that is our food security and our sure income—winter wheat feeds the household and the summer maize goes to feed and fuel money. The remaining 3 mu I plant to cotton, which brings the cash I need for school fees, medicine, and daily expenses. I buy hybrid maize seed and improved wheat varieties from the county supply shop every year; they cost more, but the yield pays for itself. Cotton I also plant with hybrid seed because the bollworm-resistant kinds save me heartbreak. Since we have a well, I irrigate the wheat three times and the maize twice when the summer rains fall short. Cotton needs the most care: I plough it deep in spring, water it three times, and spray pesticides five times because the aphids and mites never rest. For the maize after wheat, I direct-seed into the stubble with no-tillage to save time and diesel—we must get that crop in the ground within days of the wheat harvest or we lose the growing season. My fertilizers are the usual compound fertilizer plus urea; after four decades I know exactly how much gives a good crop without wasting money I do not have.
